entries.sentence: The NHS describes rheumatoid arthritis as a long-term condition that causes pain, swelling and stiffness in the joints, most often in the hands, feet and wrists.
entries.note: Search summary of NHS page: long-term condition, pain/swelling/stiffness, usually hands, feet and wrists.

entries.sentence: Joint pain, stiffness and visible swelling are the core features.
entries.note: Search summary of diagnosis/symptom pages; not attributed to one page.

entries.sentence: Symptoms often build up over several weeks, although in some people they develop over a few days.
entries.note: Summary said symptoms often build over weeks, sometimes days; page not identified.

entries.sentence: Some people also have flu-like symptoms, with a fever and muscle aches, especially around the time of diagnosis.
entries.note: Summary: flu-like symptoms with fever and muscle aches, tiredness, around diagnosis.

entries.sentence: Some people have problems in other parts of the body, or more general symptoms such as tiredness and weight loss.
entries.note: Summary of NHS page.

entries.sentence: One NHS service describes fatigue (extreme tiredness) as a very common symptom.
entries.note: Highland NHS page called fatigue a very common symptom.

entries.sentence: It notes that trying to push through fatigue and pain is likely to make both worse, so a break can help the body recover.
entries.note: Highland NHS page: pushing through makes symptoms worse; break allows recovery.

entries.sentence: A flare is a period when symptoms worsen, and NHS hospital leaflets say it can include joint pain, swelling, stiffness, tiredness and low mood.
entries.note: Kingston and Richmond leaflet: flare can include joint pain, swelling, fatigue, stiffness, low mood.

entries.sentence: Flares vary in how strong they are, how long they last and how often they happen.
entries.note: Leaflet: flares vary in intensity, duration and frequency.

entries.sentence: The same leaflet says they are usually reversible if treated promptly.
entries.note: Leaflet: usually reversible if treated promptly.

entries.sentence: Listed triggers include winding down or stopping treatment, doing too much, stress, infection and lack of sleep.
entries.note: Leaflet list of flare causes.

entries.sentence: During a flare, NHS trust advice describes gentle range-of-movement exercises rather than strength training, which puts more strain on the joints.
entries.note: Leaflet: let joints settle, range-of-movement exercises rather than strength training.

entries.sentence: Heat or cold, such as a hot water bottle, wheat bag or ice pack, may reduce pain and inflammation.
entries.note: Leaflet: heat or cold may reduce pain and inflammation.

entries.sentence: Outside flares, the NHS says regular exercise can relieve stress, keep joints mobile and strengthen the muscles that support them.
entries.note: NHS living-with page quoted in summary.

entries.sentence: It adds that an activity which makes joints warm and swollen, or causes severe pain, is a sign to stop and rest.
entries.note: NHS living-with page: if joints become warm and swollen or severe pain, stop and rest.

entries.sentence: Another trust notes that uncontrolled inflammation in a joint can lead to irreversible damage, and advises contacting the rheumatology team when regular flares carry on despite self-care.
entries.note: Summary attributed to one or more trusts: irreversible damage; seek help for regular flares lasting over a week; exact page not identified.

entries.sentence: No single test settles the diagnosis.
entries.note: Summary: no single test.

entries.sentence: Doctors usually combine an examination of the joints, blood tests and scans such as X-ray or ultrasound.
entries.note: Summary: blood tests (ESR, CRP, rheumatoid factor, anti-CCP), scans, joint examination.

entries.sentence: The blood tests can include inflammation markers (ESR and CRP) and two antibodies, rheumatoid factor and anti-CCP.
entries.note: Same summary.

entries.sentence: A positive rheumatoid factor result is not conclusive on its own.
entries.note: Summary: positive RF not conclusive on its own.

entries.sentence: People who test positive for anti-CCP are very likely to develop rheumatoid arthritis, but not everyone with the condition has this antibody.
entries.note: Summary of NRAS diagnosis page.

entries.sentence: Seropositive and seronegative are terms for whether rheumatoid factor and anti-CCP are present in the blood.
entries.note: Summary defining seropositive/seronegative; page not identified.

entries.sentence: The diagnosis is usually made by a rheumatologist, a doctor who specialises in joint and autoimmune conditions.
entries.note: Summary said diagnosis usually made by a rheumatologist; the definition of the term is general knowledge (basis kept as excerpt for the first clause only).

entries.sentence: Early diagnosis matters because medicines can ease symptoms and slow or prevent joint damage.
entries.note: Summary: early diagnosis allows medication to ease symptoms and slow or prevent damage.

entries.sentence: The NHS says treatment usually combines care from a GP with several specialists, and that medicines aim to stop the condition getting worse.
entries.note: NHS treatment page summary.

entries.sentence: The medicines are often split into two main types: disease-modifying anti-rheumatic drugs (DMARDs) and biological treatments.
entries.note: NHS treatment page summary.

entries.sentence: Methotrexate is typically the first DMARD, and it is often given with another DMARD and a short course of steroids for pain.
entries.note: NHS treatment page summary.

entries.sentence: The NHS says it can take trying two or three DMARDs to find the most suitable one, which is then usually taken long term.
entries.note: NHS treatment page summary: may have to try 2 or 3 DMARDs.

entries.sentence: Steroids, as tablets or as injections into a joint or muscle, are generally used briefly for pain relief while DMARDs take effect.
entries.note: NHS treatment page summary.

entries.sentence: Long-term steroid use can cause serious side effects, which is why courses are kept short.
entries.note: NHS treatment page summary.

entries.sentence: DMARDs themselves can have serious side effects, so frequent blood tests and other monitoring are needed.
entries.note: First search summary said DMARDs can have serious side effects and need frequent blood tests and monitoring; page not identified.

entries.sentence: Biological medicines are usually given alongside methotrexate, according to a regional NHS prescribing pathway that follows NICE criteria.
entries.note: Pathway summary: biologics and JAK inhibitors given with methotrexate unless it is not suitable.

entries.sentence: That pathway describes them as offered when at least two DMARDs, including methotrexate, have not worked or were not tolerated and disease activity stays high.
entries.note: Pathway summary of NICE criteria.

entries.sentence: JAK inhibitors are tablets, offered to people who cannot take DMARDs or biological medicines, or who tried them without benefit.
entries.note: Pathway summary.

entries.sentence: NHS inform says physiotherapy helps improve muscle strength, flexibility and fitness.
entries.note: Summary of NHS inform page.

entries.sentence: It says occupational therapy provides training and advice for people who need help with everyday tasks or have difficulty at work.
entries.note: Summary of NHS inform page.

entries.sentence: Other sources mention orthoses, which are supports worn on the body, as part of non-drug care.
entries.note: First search summary listed physical therapy, orthoses and occupational therapy; page not identified; definition of orthoses is general.

entries.sentence: Some people need surgery to replace part or all of a joint, such as the hip, knee or shoulder.
entries.note: Summary of NHS inform page.

entries.sentence: The NHS also covers operations that correct joint problems in the hand.
entries.note: Summary said NHS covers hand surgery types; page not identified precisely.

entries.sentence: NHS guidance says early treatment and support can reduce the risk of joint damage and limit the impact of the condition.
entries.note: Summary of NHS pages.

entries.sentence: The NHS describes rheumatoid arthritis as a condition with no cure, but treatment can ease symptoms and limit joint damage.
entries.note: Summary: long-term, no cure, treatment helps.

entries.sentence: A review describes it as a systemic disease, meaning it can affect the whole body, with complications from the condition and from its treatment.
entries.note: PMC7356332: RA is a systemic disease; systemic manifestations and treatment-related complications.

entries.sentence: Lumps in the lung called rheumatoid nodules often cause no symptoms and tend to settle on their own.
entries.note: PMC7356332: lung nodules usually asymptomatic and tend to resolve.

entries.sentence: Heart-related problems such as inflammation of the heart muscle or lining, and a protein build-up called amyloidosis, are described as relatively rare.
entries.note: PMC7356332: endocarditis, myocarditis, amyloidosis relatively rare.

entries.sentence: Arthritis in the joint at the top of the neck can wear away part of the bone beneath it.
entries.note: PMC7356332: atlantoaxial arthritis can erode the odontoid process.

entries.sentence: Studies link early, closely monitored treatment with a better long-term course and less structural damage to joints.
entries.note: Search summary: early tight control linked to better course and less damage; page not identified.

entries.sentence: Lasting remission, meaning disease that is quiet, is reached by only a minority of people, and remission without any medicine is described as rare.
entries.note: Search summary of PMC reviews/cohorts; exact page not identified.

entries.sentence: The NHS describes rheumatoid arthritis as a long-term condition with no cure at present.
entries.note: Summary of NHS pages.

entries.sentence: Treatment can ease symptoms and limit joint damage, and the sources stress that starting early gives the best chance of that.
entries.note: Summary: early treatment can reduce risk of damage and limit impact.

entries.sentence: Some people reach remission, meaning the disease is quiet, but this is described as happening to a minority.
entries.note: Search summary; page not identified.

entries.sentence: Seropositive means rheumatoid factor or anti-CCP antibodies are found in the blood.
entries.note: Summary defining seropositive.

entries.sentence: Seronegative means they are not found.
entries.note: Summary defining seronegative.

entries.sentence: A positive rheumatoid factor is not conclusive alone, and not everyone with the condition has anti-CCP, so doctors look at the whole picture.
entries.note: Summary of NRAS page.

entries.sentence: DMARDs can have serious side effects, so frequent blood tests and other monitoring are described as part of taking them.
entries.note: First search summary; page not identified.

entries.sentence: Blood tests are also used when the condition is first being diagnosed, to look for signs of inflammation and for particular antibodies.
entries.note: Summary of diagnosis pages.

entries.sentence: The joints are the main target, but some people have problems in other parts of the body or more general symptoms such as tiredness and weight loss, according to the NHS.
entries.note: Summary of NHS page.

entries.sentence: A review describes it as a systemic disease, meaning it can involve the whole body.
NHS inform says some people need surgery to replace part or all of a joint, such as the hip, knee or shoulder.
entries.note: Summary of NHS inform page.

entries.sentence: Surgery is one of several supports alongside medicines, physiotherapy and occupational therapy, and the sources do not describe it as needed by everyone.
entries.note: Summary lists surgery among options; 'not needed by everyone' is implied by 'some people' wording.

entries.sentence: NHS hospital leaflets list winding down or stopping treatment, doing too much, stress, infection and lack of sleep.
entries.note: Leaflet list.

entries.sentence: They say flares vary in strength and length and are usually reversible if treated promptly, and they advise contacting the rheumatology team if regular flares continue despite self-care.
entries.note: Leaflet summary; contact advice attributed to trust pages generally.

entries.sentence: RA
entries.note: Existing entry alias; NHS page title uses the name rheumatoid arthritis.

entries.sentence: A long-term condition with no cure at present, according to the NHS
entries.note: Summary of NHS pages.

entries.sentence: Hands, feet and wrists
entries.note: Summary of NHS page.

entries.sentence: No single test; blood tests, scans and a joint examination are combined
entries.note: Summary.

entries.sentence: DMARDs and biological treatments, with short steroid courses for pain
entries.note: NHS treatment page summary.

entries.sentence: Methotrexate, often with another DMARD
entries.note: NHS treatment page summary.

entries.sentence: A rheumatologist usually makes the diagnosis
entries.note: Summary.

contradictions: Existing overview says 'disease-modifying drugs now prevent most damage' and calls DMARDs 'recommended early for every patient'; retrieved text only says treatment can ease symptoms and slow or prevent damage, and describes no cure and that remission is reached by a minority. Wording 'prevent most damage' not supported by retrieved text.
